title: Tariffs are becoming a lived consumer signal through visible price increases, product-value judgments, safety trust, and political attribution
source_unit: Ipsos Consumer Tracker wave released 28 September 2026, including tariff perceptions, clothing-value judgments, food-inspection trust, community safety, and consumer technology use
geography: United States adults age 18 and older; recurring Ipsos online Consumer Tracker with current wave focused on tariff and consumer perceptions

observations.period: 28 September 2026; latest Ipsos Consumer Tracker wave

tariff_price_expectation.unit: percent of Americans agreeing tariffs will raise prices on goods they buy

tariff_price_exposure.unit: percent saying they have already seen prices rise specifically because of tariffs

historical_shift.value: the corresponding figures were 66% for expected price increases in January 2025 and 43% for observed tariff-linked price increases in February 2025

consumer_conversion.value: trade policy is being interpreted through household prices rather than remaining an abstract policy instrument

observations.method: Ipsos recurring Consumer Tracker; the public page summarizes current-wave results and historical comparisons but does not provide a causal tariff-incidence estimate.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived tariff-linked price increases are not a product-level price index and do not establish the share of price changes caused by tariffs; the summary does not provide the full sample or weighting details for this wave on the landing page.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers with different incomes, purchasing baskets, political identities, import exposure, geographic markets, and ability to substitute or delay purchases.
observations.counterinterpretation: Consumers can accurately perceive a price increase without identifying its cause, and tariff attribution can coexist with other inflation, supply-chain, exchange-rate, or firm-pricing effects.

observations.period: September 2026; tariffs, product value, and substitution

denominator.unit: Ipsos current Consumer Tracker thematic module

value_judgment.value: the wave examines clothing-value perceptions, including cost-per-wear as a purchase metric among younger Americans

purchase_mechanism.value: visible price pressure can move consumer judgment from sticker price toward durability, repeat use, and total value

room_route.value: product longevity and substitution may protect household room, but can also require higher up-front spending or exclude consumers with limited liquidity

outcome_boundary.value: the public summary does not establish actual purchase changes, apparel quality, household savings, or reduced consumption

observations.method: Ipsos thematic consumer-attitudes module summarized on the tracker page; the landing page does not provide a full cross-tabulation or observed purchase data.
observations.uncertainty: The phrase cost per wear describes a reported decision criterion, not a measured lifecycle calculation or causal response to tariffs.
observations.subgroup: Younger consumers, low-liquidity households, value-conscious shoppers, apparel firms, resale markets, and consumers facing different price and quality options.
observations.counterinterpretation: Value language can support more durable consumption, but it can also rationalize paying more for premium goods or shift responsibility for affordability onto consumers.

observations.period: September 2026; consumer trust in public safety systems

denominator.unit: Ipsos current Consumer Tracker thematic module

food_inspection.value: the wave examines whether Americans trust food-safety inspections, with the public summary noting a separate finding that most Americans trust food inspections less

community_safety.value: the wave also examines community safety and perceptions of armed federal agents

institutional_route.value: consumer trust in market and public-safety institutions can shape perceived legitimacy of prices, protection, and enforcement

evidence_boundary.value: the public page does not provide the full percentages, question wording, subgroup differences, or observed food-safety outcomes in the summary itself

observations.method: Ipsos public summary of a recurring online tracker and linked topical releases; no administrative inspection or crime outcome is included in this record.
observations.uncertainty: Trust measures may respond to media exposure, political conflict, personal experience, or institutional performance, and the public summary does not separate those pathways.
observations.subgroup: Consumers, parents, food purchasers, communities exposed to different safety risks, and people with different trust in federal and local institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower trust does not prove inspection failure; it may reflect generalized institutional skepticism or disagreement about enforcement authority.

observations.period: September 2026; policy perception, attribution, and consumer action

political_attribution.value: tariff-linked price perceptions create a route through which trade policy can be judged through household purchasing experience

firm_response.value: firms may face consumer pressure to explain price changes, preserve value, and demonstrate safety or fairness

consumer_action.value: the open question is whether perceived price causes translate into substitution, reduced quantity, delayed purchase, brand switching, political preference, or complaint

causal_boundary.value: the tracker provides attitudes and perceptions, not a causal estimate linking tariffs to purchases, votes, or institutional trust

observations.method: Bounded synthesis of the Ipsos tracker’s tariff, value, safety, and consumer-behavior modules.
observations.uncertainty: The landing page does not identify whether the same respondent changed behavior or political judgment after observing a price increase.
observations.subgroup: Consumers, firms, policymakers, trade-exposed workers, and households with different ability to absorb or avoid price changes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Consumers can report tariff concern without changing purchases or political behavior, especially when necessities have few substitutes.

related_sources.claim: Ipsos Consumer Tracker landing page, current wave, linked modules, and methodology route.
Official September 29, 2026 Ipsos release directly reports the tariff understanding, higher-price expectation, worth-it, and jobs-benefit measures summarized in this record.

boundary: This record adds a tariff-to-consumer-politics route: trade policy becomes socially legible through perceived price increases, product value, public safety, institutional trust, and household substitution. It uses Ipsos’s public tracker summary, not product-level price data, causal tariff incidence, observed purchasing, administrative inspection outcomes, or proof of political behavior.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Ipsos tracker page reviewed for 28 September 2026 release date, 81% and 71% tariff-price figures, January 2025 and February 2025 comparisons, cost-per-wear, food-inspection trust, community safety, and linked methodology.
